topics.name: Introduction to Pediatrics, vital signs, general examination, communication and ethics

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the central focus of pediatrics?

options.label: A
options.text: Care of infants, children and adolescents, including prevention, growth, development and disease

options.label: C
options.text: Management of children until the neonatal period ends

options.label: D
options.text: Care limited to prescribing medication according to body weight

options.label: E
options.text: Management of diseases in children after symptoms become severe

questions.correctAnswerText: Care of infants, children and adolescents, including prevention, growth, development and disease
questions.initialExplanation: Pediatrics addresses the health of the developing child across age groups. It combines prevention, health promotion, surveillance of growth and development, diagnosis, treatment, rehabilitation and family-centred care.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Correct. This captures the broad scope of pediatric medicine and the importance of development and prevention. 
- B: Incorrect. Congenital conditions form only one part of pediatrics. 
- C: Incorrect. Pediatrics extends well beyond the neonatal period and includes childhood and adolescence. 
- D: Incorrect. Weight-based prescribing is important but is only one component of pediatric practice.

- E: Incorrect. Pediatric care includes anticipatory guidance, prevention and early recognition, not only severe symptomatic disease.
questions.highYieldPoints: A child is not simply a small adult. Age, development, physiology, family context and safeguarding all influence pediatric assessment.

source.raw: General Pediatrics & Clinical Skills — Introduction to Pediatrics.

questions.stem: Why should growth and development be assessed routinely during pediatric visits?

options.label: A
options.text: They can reveal chronic disease, nutritional problems or developmental disorders before obvious symptoms appear

options.label: B
options.text: They are useful during the first year of life

options.label: C
options.text: They determine the child's blood group

options.label: D
options.text: They replace the need for a medical history

options.label: E
options.text: They are relevant when a child has a neurological disorder

questions.correctAnswerText: They can reveal chronic disease, nutritional problems or developmental disorders before obvious symptoms appear
questions.initialExplanation: Serial measurements and developmental surveillance can identify faltering growth, endocrine or systemic disease, nutritional deficiency and developmental delay. A single measurement is less informative than a trajectory over time.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Correct. Abnormal trajectories can be early clues to significant disease or unmet developmental needs. 
- B: Incorrect. Surveillance remains important throughout childhood and adolescence. 
- C: Incorrect. Growth and development do not determine blood group.

- D: Incorrect. Growth assessment complements, rather than replaces, history and examination. 
- E: Incorrect. Growth and development are core measures for every child, not only children with neurological disease.
questions.highYieldPoints: Interpret height, weight and head circumference against age- and sex-appropriate charts; assess trends rather than isolated values.

source.raw: General Pediatrics & Clinical Skills — Introduction to Pediatrics / General Examination.

questions.stem: Which approach is most appropriate when assessing a child's vital signs?

options.label: A
options.text: Interpret most values using adult reference ranges

options.label: B
options.text: Record values without documenting the child's age or clinical state

options.label: C
options.text: Regard tachycardia as diagnostic of sepsis

options.label: D
options.text: Interpret vital signs using age-appropriate ranges and the child's overall condition

options.label: E
options.text: Measure respiratory rate when respiratory symptoms are present

questions.correctAnswerText: Interpret vital signs using age-appropriate ranges and the child's overall condition
questions.initialExplanation: Normal heart rate, respiratory rate and blood pressure vary substantially with age. Fever, crying, pain, activity and distress can also affect measurements, so values must be interpreted in context.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Incorrect. Adult ranges are inappropriate for infants and children. 
- B: Incorrect. Age and clinical context are essential to interpretation. 
- C: Incorrect. Tachycardia is nonspecific and may occur with fever, dehydration, pain, anxiety or many other conditions. 
- D: Correct. Age-specific reference ranges and the full clinical picture should guide interpretation. 
- E: Incorrect. Respiratory rate is a core vital sign and may reveal early deterioration even without reported respiratory symptoms.
questions.highYieldPoints: Count respiratory rate while the child is calm when possible; assess work of breathing, perfusion, mental state and hydration alongside numerical observations.

source.raw: General Pediatrics & Clinical Skills — Pediatric Vital Signs Assessment.

questions.stem: Which finding is most useful when assessing peripheral perfusion in a child?

options.label: D
options.text: Capillary refill time, interpreted with skin temperature and pulse quality

questions.correctAnswerText: Capillary refill time, interpreted with skin temperature and pulse quality
questions.initialExplanation: Capillary refill time is a bedside indicator of peripheral perfusion. It should be considered with extremity temperature, pulse volume, skin colour, mental state and urine output.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Incorrect. Visual acuity does not assess systemic circulation. 
- B: Incorrect. Hair colour does not assess circulation. 
- C: Incorrect. Abdominal circumference may be useful in selected conditions but is not a direct perfusion measure.

- D: Correct. Capillary refill and associated perfusion signs help identify circulatory compromise. 
- E: Incorrect. Dentition may contribute to developmental assessment but not perfusion.
questions.highYieldPoints: A prolonged refill time, cold mottled extremities, weak pulses and altered consciousness are concerning, especially when they occur together.

source.raw: General Pediatrics & Clinical Skills — Pediatric Vital Signs Assessment / General Examination.

questions.stem: Which is the best initial principle when examining an anxious or frightened child?

options.label: A
options.text: Establish rapport, explain what will happen and use an age-appropriate approach

options.label: B
options.text: Separate the child from the caregiver in each case

options.label: C
options.text: Complete the examination without involving the caregiver

options.label: D
options.text: Ignore the child's behaviour because it is not clinically relevant

options.label: E
options.text: Begin immediately with the most invasive part of the examination

questions.correctAnswerText: Establish rapport, explain what will happen and use an age-appropriate approach
questions.initialExplanation: A calm, developmentally appropriate approach improves cooperation and examination quality. The caregiver can provide reassurance and important historical information, while the child's assent and comfort should be respected.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Correct. Rapport and explanation improve cooperation and reduce distress. 
- B: Incorrect. Caregiver presence is usually helpful, although circumstances and the child's age may require private discussion. 
- C: Incorrect. Caregivers are important partners in pediatric assessment, subject to confidentiality and safeguarding considerations.

- D: Incorrect. Behaviour may reflect pain, developmental status, fear or altered consciousness. 
- E: Incorrect. Invasive or distressing procedures are generally deferred until necessary and after rapport has been established.
questions.highYieldPoints: Observe before touching; perform less distressing parts first; leave ears, mouth and other upsetting elements until later when feasible.

source.raw: General Pediatrics & Clinical Skills — General Examination / Communication Skills.

questions.stem: Which communication strategy is most appropriate when taking a history from a caregiver?

options.label: A
options.text: Begin with an open question, then clarify details using focused questions

options.label: B
options.text: Use technical language to demonstrate expertise

options.label: C
options.text: Ask several unrelated questions at the same time

options.label: E
options.text: Interrupt frequently to correct the caregiver

questions.correctAnswerText: Begin with an open question, then clarify details using focused questions
questions.initialExplanation: Open questions allow the caregiver to describe the presenting concern in their own words. Focused questions then clarify onset, duration, progression, associated symptoms, risk factors and impact on the child.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Correct. This combines an open narrative with structured clinical clarification. 
- B: Incorrect. Clear, accessible language is preferable to unnecessary jargon. 
- C: Incorrect. Multiple questions at once can confuse the caregiver and make the history incomplete. 
- D: Incorrect. Closed questions are useful for clarification but should not replace the initial narrative.

- E: Incorrect. Frequent interruption can damage rapport and cause important details to be missed.
questions.highYieldPoints: Listen actively, clarify ambiguous details, summarize the history back to the caregiver and check understanding.

source.raw: General Pediatrics & Clinical Skills — Communication Skills.

questions.stem: What is the most appropriate response when a caregiver does not understand a proposed investigation?

options.label: A
options.text: Explain the purpose, expected benefits, relevant risks and alternatives in understandable language

options.label: B
options.text: Ask the child to obtain consent from the caregiver

options.label: D
options.text: Repeat the same technical explanation more loudly

options.label: E
options.text: Avoid discussing risks because they may cause anxiety

questions.correctAnswerText: Explain the purpose, expected benefits, relevant risks and alternatives in understandable language
questions.initialExplanation: Valid consent requires adequate information and understanding. Communication should be tailored to the caregiver's language, health literacy and concerns, while involving the child according to age and maturity.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Correct. A balanced explanation supports informed decision-making. 
- B: Incorrect. A child should not be made responsible for obtaining parental consent. 
- C: Incorrect. Proceeding without appropriate consent is not acceptable except in narrowly defined emergencies. 
- D: Incorrect. Volume does not correct a communication or health-literacy problem. 
- E: Incorrect. Material risks should be discussed honestly and proportionately.
questions.highYieldPoints: Consent is a communication process, not merely a signature.

source.raw: General Pediatrics & Clinical Skills — Communication Skills / Medical Ethics.

questions.stem: Which principle is fundamental when making decisions about a child's healthcare?

options.label: A
options.text: The best interests of the child should guide decisions

options.label: B
options.text: Children should not usually be involved in decisions

options.label: C
options.text: The caregiver's preference automatically overrides each other consideration

options.label: D
options.text: Confidentiality is absolute even when a child is at serious risk of harm

options.label: E
options.text: The clinician's convenience typically takes priority

questions.correctAnswerText: The best interests of the child should guide decisions
questions.initialExplanation: The child's best interests are central to pediatric decision-making. Parents or guardians generally make decisions for younger children, but the child's views and evolving capacity should be considered.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Correct. Best interests guide clinical and ethical decisions concerning children. 
- B: Incorrect. Children should be involved in a developmentally appropriate way. 
- C: Incorrect. Parental authority is important but is not unlimited when a decision exposes a child to serious harm. 
- D: Incorrect. Confidentiality may need to be breached when necessary to protect a child from serious harm, following applicable law and policy.

- E: Incorrect. Convenience is not a valid substitute for the child's welfare.
questions.highYieldPoints: Consider best interests, parental responsibility, the child's developing capacity, assent, confidentiality and safeguarding.

source.raw: General Pediatrics & Clinical Skills — Medical Ethics.

questions.stem: What is the most appropriate action if the history and physical findings raise concern for possible child maltreatment?

options.label: A
options.text: Document objective findings carefully and follow the local safeguarding pathway

options.label: B
options.text: Discharge the child without further assessment

options.label: C
options.text: Promise the child that no information will ever be shared

options.label: D
options.text: Confront the caregiver aggressively in front of the child

options.label: E
options.text: Ignore the concern unless the caregiver admits abuse

questions.correctAnswerText: Document objective findings carefully and follow the local safeguarding pathway
questions.initialExplanation: Safeguarding concerns require careful, factual documentation, assessment of immediate safety and escalation through established child-protection procedures. Avoid leading questions and avoid making unsupported accusations.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Correct. Objective documentation and formal safeguarding procedures protect the child and preserve evidence. 
- B: Incorrect. A child at risk may require urgent protection and multidisciplinary review. 
- C: Incorrect. Absolute promises of secrecy are inappropriate when disclosure may be needed for safety.

- D: Incorrect. Aggressive confrontation may increase risk and compromise assessment. 
- E: Incorrect. A disclosure is not required before concerns can be assessed or escalated.
questions.highYieldPoints: Record what was seen and said, distinguishing direct quotations from interpretation. Follow institutional and legal requirements.

questions.stem: Why is the caregiver's account especially important in pediatric history-taking?

options.label: A
options.text: Caregivers may describe the child's baseline function, symptom chronology and changes from normal behaviour

options.label: C
options.text: Caregivers can reliably diagnose the underlying disease

options.label: D
options.text: The caregiver's account typically replaces physical examination

options.label: E
options.text: The child should not usually be asked questions

questions.correctAnswerText: Caregivers may describe the child's baseline function, symptom chronology and changes from normal behaviour
questions.initialExplanation: Caregivers often know the child's usual behaviour, feeding, development, activity and symptom timeline. The child should still be involved where appropriate, and the account should be interpreted alongside examination and investigations.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Correct. A caregiver can identify deviations from the child's normal baseline. 
- B: Incorrect. Children can provide valuable information depending on age, development and clinical state. 
- C: Incorrect. Caregivers provide observations, not a definitive medical diagnosis.

- D: Incorrect. History does not replace examination. 
- E: Incorrect. Children should be addressed directly in an age-appropriate manner.
questions.highYieldPoints: Ask both the caregiver and the child when developmentally appropriate; discrepancies may themselves require clarification.

source.raw: General Pediatrics & Clinical Skills — Introduction / Communication Skills.

questions.stem: Which component belongs to a structured general pediatric examination?

options.label: A
options.text: Examination of the painful joint in each presentation

options.label: B
options.text: Assessment of appearance, growth, vital signs and hydration

options.label: C
options.text: Examination limited to the cardiovascular system

options.label: D
options.text: Recording weight without plotting it on an appropriate chart

questions.correctAnswerText: Assessment of appearance, growth, vital signs and hydration
questions.initialExplanation: A general pediatric examination begins with observation of the child's overall appearance and includes vital signs, anthropometry, hydration, nutritional state and a systematic examination guided by the presenting problem.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Incorrect. A focused examination is important, but a general assessment may reveal systemic disease or red flags. 
- B: Correct. These domains provide a broad initial picture of the child's condition. 
- C: Incorrect. A complete general examination is not restricted to one system.

- D: Incorrect. Weight should be interpreted in relation to age, sex and previous measurements. 
- E: Incorrect. Developmental and behavioural observations are relevant to pediatric assessment.
questions.highYieldPoints: Start with observation and vital signs, then perform a systematic examination and focused assessment.

source.raw: General Pediatrics & Clinical Skills — General Examination.

questions.stem: Which statement about blood pressure measurement in children is most accurate?

options.label: A
options.text: Correct cuff size and age-appropriate interpretation are essential

options.label: B
options.text: A cuff that is too small tends to underestimate blood pressure

options.label: C
options.text: One elevated reading typically establishes persistent hypertension

options.label: D
options.text: A cuff that is too large tends to overestimate blood pressure

options.label: E
options.text: Blood pressure is not usually required in an asymptomatic child

questions.correctAnswerText: Correct cuff size and age-appropriate interpretation are essential
questions.initialExplanation: Correct cuff size is essential for reliable pediatric blood pressure measurement. A cuff that is too small tends to overestimate, while one that is too large may underestimate the reading. Interpretation depends on age, sex and height in children.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Correct. Technique and reference standards both matter. 
- B: Incorrect. A cuff that is too small generally gives a falsely high reading. 
- C: Incorrect. Persistent hypertension requires repeated, properly measured elevated readings.

- D: Incorrect. An excessively large cuff may give a falsely low reading. 
- E: Incorrect. Routine screening is recommended in appropriate age groups and clinical settings.
questions.highYieldPoints: Cuff width is approximately 40% of mid-upper arm circumference; bladder length should cover about 80–100% of arm circumference. See the detailed hypertension section for standard guidance-specific measurement summary.

source.raw: General Pediatrics & Clinical Skills — Vital Signs; Childhood Hypertension, pp. 12–18.

questions.stem: Which measurement is most useful for monitoring linear growth over time?

options.label: A
options.text: Serial standing height or recumbent length plotted on an appropriate growth chart

options.label: B
options.text: A single random blood glucose measurement

options.label: C
options.text: Mid-arm circumference in each age group

questions.correctAnswerText: Serial standing height or recumbent length plotted on an appropriate growth chart
questions.initialExplanation: Serial height or length measurements show the child's linear growth trajectory. Measurements should be accurate, age-appropriate and interpreted with weight, BMI and family growth pattern.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Correct. Serial length/height is the direct measure of linear growth. 
- B: Incorrect. Blood glucose does not measure growth. 
- C: Incorrect. Mid-upper arm circumference can help assess nutritional status but is not the universal measure of linear growth. 
- D: Incorrect. Head circumference is important, particularly in younger children, but does not measure linear growth. 
- E: Incorrect. Chest circumference is not a standard substitute for height/length.
questions.highYieldPoints: A growth chart is most useful when serial, accurately measured values are available.

source.raw: Growth, Nutrition & Development — Common Nutritional Disorders / Short Stature.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes failure to thrive (FTT) or faltering growth?

options.label: A
options.text: It describes inadequate weight gain or growth relative to the child's expected trajectory

options.label: B
options.text: It is exclusively caused by inadequate parental feeding

options.label: D
options.text: It is synonymous with short stature

options.label: E
options.text: A single low weight measurement typically establishes FTT

questions.correctAnswerText: It describes inadequate weight gain or growth relative to the child's expected trajectory
questions.initialExplanation: FTT is a clinical description of poor weight gain or a downward deviation in growth trajectory. Assessment should consider nutritional intake, feeding difficulties, chronic disease, psychosocial factors and measurement accuracy.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Correct. The pattern of growth over time is central. 
- B: Incorrect. Causes may be nutritional, medical, developmental or psychosocial. 
- C: Incorrect. Faltering growth can occur in infancy and childhood.

- D: Incorrect. Weight faltering and reduced linear growth can coexist but are not identical. 
- E: Incorrect. A single measurement may reflect constitutional small size or error; serial trajectory is important.
questions.highYieldPoints: Consider inadequate intake, malabsorption, increased metabolic demand, chronic illness and psychosocial contributors.

source.raw: Growth, Nutrition & Development — Common Nutritional Disorders, FTT section.

questions.stem: Which pattern most strongly suggests an organic cause of faltering growth?

options.label: A
options.text: Recurrent vomiting, chronic diarrhoea, systemic symptoms or abnormal examination findings

options.label: B
options.text: Normal examination with a clear history of low energy intake and no other symptoms

options.label: D
options.text: Normal development and normal growth velocity

options.label: E
options.text: A stable low centile that follows the family's pattern

questions.correctAnswerText: Recurrent vomiting, chronic diarrhoea, systemic symptoms or abnormal examination findings
questions.initialExplanation: Persistent gastrointestinal symptoms, systemic illness, abnormal examination findings or evidence of chronic disease support investigation for an organic cause.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Correct. These findings raise concern for gastrointestinal, inflammatory, metabolic or other medical pathology. 
- B: Incorrect. Low intake may cause faltering growth, but this history alone does not establish an organic disease. 
- C: Incorrect. Measurement error should be checked, not interpreted as disease.

- D: Incorrect. Normal development and growth velocity are reassuring rather than suggestive of organic disease. 
- E: Incorrect. A stable trajectory consistent with familial pattern may be normal.
questions.highYieldPoints: Always assess dietary intake and feeding technique, but look for evidence of malabsorption, chronic infection, cardiac/renal disease and endocrine disorders.

source.raw: Growth, Nutrition & Development — Common Nutritional Disorders.

questions.stem: Which feature is characteristic of marasmus?

options.label: A
options.text: Normal weight with isolated hair changes

options.label: B
options.text: Marked fatty liver as the clinical feature

options.label: C
options.text: Severe wasting with loss of subcutaneous fat and muscle

options.label: D
options.text: Excessive adipose tissue with normal muscle bulk

options.label: E
options.text: Generalized oedema as the defining feature

questions.correctAnswerText: Severe wasting with loss of subcutaneous fat and muscle
questions.initialExplanation: Marasmus results from severe energy deficiency and presents with marked wasting, loss of muscle and subcutaneous fat, and a very low body weight. Oedema is not the defining feature.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Incorrect. This does not describe severe protein-energy malnutrition. 
- B: Incorrect. Fatty liver may occur in kwashiorkor and is not the sole feature of marasmus. 
- C: Correct. Severe wasting is the hallmark of marasmus. 
- D: Incorrect. This describes neither marasmus nor a severe wasting syndrome.

- E: Incorrect. Generalized oedema is classically associated with kwashiorkor.
questions.highYieldPoints: Marasmus = severe wasting; kwashiorkor = oedema in the setting of protein-energy malnutrition. Mixed presentations occur.

source.raw: Growth, Nutrition & Development — Common Nutritional Disorders, PEM section.

questions.stem: Which finding is most characteristic of kwashiorkor?

options.label: C
options.text: Bilateral pitting oedema in a child with protein-energy malnutrition

questions.correctAnswerText: Bilateral pitting oedema in a child with protein-energy malnutrition
questions.initialExplanation: Oedema is the key clinical feature distinguishing kwashiorkor from uncomplicated marasmus. Other findings may include skin and hair changes, apathy, poor appetite and hepatomegaly.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Incorrect. Severe wasting without oedema is more typical of marasmus. 
- B: Incorrect. This suggests a possible diabetic presentation, not kwashiorkor. 
- C: Correct. Bilateral pitting oedema is the defining clinical clue. 
- D: Incorrect. Microcephaly is not a defining feature of kwashiorkor. 
- E: Incorrect. Protein-energy malnutrition causes impaired growth and function, not increased muscle mass.
questions.highYieldPoints: Oedema may mask weight loss. Assess nutritional status, complications and infection risk rather than relying on weight alone.

source.raw: Growth, Nutrition & Development — Common Nutritional Disorders, PEM section.

questions.stem: Why must a child with severe acute malnutrition be refed cautiously?

options.label: C
options.text: Because nutritional rehabilitation is not usually indicated

options.label: D
options.text: To prevent refeeding-related electrolyte and metabolic disturbances

options.label: E
options.text: Because carbohydrates cannot be absorbed in childhood

questions.correctAnswerText: To prevent refeeding-related electrolyte and metabolic disturbances
questions.initialExplanation: Refeeding after prolonged malnutrition can trigger insulin-mediated intracellular shifts of phosphate, potassium and magnesium. This can cause arrhythmias, cardiac dysfunction, neurological complications and fluid imbalance.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Incorrect. Protein is required for recovery, but overall feeding should follow an appropriate stabilization and rehabilitation plan. 
- B: Incorrect. Supporting catch-up growth is a major treatment objective.

- C: Incorrect. Nutritional rehabilitation is essential. 
- D: Correct. Careful staged nutritional rehabilitation reduces the risk of refeeding syndrome. 
- E: Incorrect. Carbohydrates are absorbed normally in most children; the issue is the metabolic response to refeeding.
questions.highYieldPoints: Correct and monitor electrolyte disturbances, especially phosphate, potassium and magnesium, in high-risk children.

source.raw: Growth, Nutrition & Development — Common Nutritional Disorders, treatment/refeeding section.

questions.stem: Which is a major potential complication of childhood obesity?

options.label: A
options.text: Insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes risk

questions.correctAnswerText: Insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes risk
questions.initialExplanation: Childhood obesity is associated with insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, dyslipidaemia, hypertension, fatty liver disease, obstructive sleep apnoea and psychosocial consequences.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Correct. Insulin resistance is a central metabolic complication. 
- B: Incorrect. Obesity increases rather than reduces the risk of hypertension. 
- C: Incorrect. Obesity increases the risk of metabolic dysfunction-associated fatty liver disease. 
- D: Incorrect. Dyslipidaemia is a recognized associated risk. 
- E: Incorrect. Obesity increases the risk of sleep-disordered breathing.
questions.highYieldPoints: Assess comorbidities, family habits, nutrition, activity, sleep and psychosocial health; management should be family-centred and non-stigmatizing.

source.raw: Growth, Nutrition & Development — Common Nutritional Disorders, obesity section.

questions.stem: Which principle is most appropriate when planning treatment for childhood obesity?

options.label: A
options.text: Restrict most dietary fat in children in routine care

options.label: B
options.text: Avoid discussing sleep and sedentary time

options.label: C
options.text: Use a family-centred approach involving nutrition, physical activity and sustainable behavioural change

options.label: E
options.text: Prescribe medication as the first intervention for children in routine care

questions.correctAnswerText: Use a family-centred approach involving nutrition, physical activity and sustainable behavioural change
questions.initialExplanation: Lifestyle and family-based interventions are foundational. The aim is healthier behaviours and improved metabolic health, with an age- and severity-appropriate plan and monitoring of growth.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Incorrect. Balanced nutrition is required; blanket elimination of dietary fat is inappropriate. 
- B: Incorrect. Sleep and sedentary habits influence weight and metabolic health. 
- C: Correct. Sustainable family-based change addresses the environment in which the child eats, moves and sleeps. 
- D: Incorrect. Rapid weight loss may be unsafe and is not the sole objective in a growing child. 
- E: Incorrect. Medication is reserved for selected circumstances and is not universal first-line treatment.
questions.highYieldPoints: Avoid stigma, assess comorbidities and involve caregivers in practical, achievable changes.

source.raw: Growth, Nutrition & Development — Common Nutritional Disorders, obesity management.

questions.stem: Which finding is most consistent with vitamin D deficiency in a growing child?

options.label: B
options.text: Rickets with impaired mineralization of growing bone

questions.correctAnswerText: Rickets with impaired mineralization of growing bone
questions.initialExplanation: Vitamin D deficiency impairs calcium and phosphate homeostasis and can cause defective mineralization of growing bone, producing rickets in children.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Incorrect. Vitamin D deficiency does not cause bacterial meningitis. 
- B: Correct. Rickets is the classic pediatric skeletal manifestation. 
- C: Incorrect. Renal agenesis is a congenital structural anomaly. 
- D: Incorrect. Hyperthyroidism is unrelated to the defining skeletal pathology of rickets.

- E: Incorrect. Haematuria is a urinary finding and is not a typical direct manifestation of vitamin D deficiency.
questions.highYieldPoints: Consider dietary intake, sunlight exposure, malabsorption, chronic liver or renal disease and relevant biochemical abnormalities.

source.raw: Growth, Nutrition & Development — Common Nutritional Disorders, vitamin deficiency section.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes developmental surveillance?

options.label: A
options.text: It should be postponed until school age

options.label: B
options.text: It is a single formal test performed when delay is suspected

options.label: C
options.text: It is an ongoing process using caregiver concerns, observation and developmental history at routine contacts

options.label: E
options.text: It is limited to assessing speech

questions.correctAnswerText: It is an ongoing process using caregiver concerns, observation and developmental history at routine contacts
questions.initialExplanation: Developmental surveillance is continuous and occurs at routine health contacts. It includes caregiver concerns, developmental history, observation and review of milestone attainment.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Incorrect. Early surveillance is important because timely intervention can improve outcomes.

- B: Incorrect. A formal screen or diagnostic assessment may be required, but surveillance is ongoing. 
- C: Correct. It is an integrated, repeated process. 
- D: Incorrect. Surveillance may identify the need for formal screening or full assessment; it does not replace them. 
- E: Incorrect. Gross motor, fine motor, language/hearing and social-adaptive domains are considered.
questions.highYieldPoints: Ask about parental concerns and regression; loss of previously acquired skills is particularly concerning.

source.raw: Growth, Nutrition & Development — Developmental Assessment, introductory slides.

questions.stem: Which set correctly lists the four broad developmental domains commonly assessed?

options.label: A
options.text: Gross motor, fine motor, language/hearing and personal-social development

options.label: C
options.text: Height, weight, temperature and blood pressure

options.label: D
options.text: Vision, dentition, reflexes and skin colour

options.label: E
options.text: Memory, appetite, sleep and bowel habit

questions.correctAnswerText: Gross motor, fine motor, language/hearing and personal-social development
questions.initialExplanation: Developmental assessment commonly examines gross motor, fine motor/adaptive, language/hearing and personal-social domains.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Correct. These are the standard broad developmental domains. 
- B: Incorrect. These are organ systems, not developmental domains. 
- C: Incorrect. These are anthropometric/vital observations. 
- D: Incorrect. These are examination findings and do not replace developmental domains.

- E: Incorrect. Some may be clinically relevant but do not represent the four broad domains.
questions.highYieldPoints: A child may be delayed in one domain or several. Document the pattern, severity and functional impact.

source.raw: Growth, Nutrition & Development — Developmental Assessment.

questions.stem: Which statement about developmental milestones is most accurate?

options.label: A
options.text: Milestones are interpreted as age-related ranges, and the overall developmental pattern matters

options.label: B
options.text: Milestones are useful for predicting adult intelligence

options.label: C
options.text: Regression is less important than delayed acquisition

options.label: D
options.text: A single missed milestone typically confirms a specific neurological diagnosis

options.label: E
options.text: children in routine care acquires each milestone on exactly the same day

questions.correctAnswerText: Milestones are interpreted as age-related ranges, and the overall developmental pattern matters
questions.initialExplanation: Developmental milestones vary within expected age ranges. Assessment should consider the overall trajectory, multiple domains, clinical context and any loss of acquired skills.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Correct. Milestones are guides, not rigid deadlines. 
- B: Incorrect. Milestones assess current functional development, not simply adult intelligence prediction. 
- C: Incorrect. Regression is a red flag and often warrants urgent evaluation.

- D: Incorrect. One delayed milestone prompts assessment but does not independently establish a specific diagnosis. 
- E: Incorrect. Normal developmental timing varies between children.
questions.highYieldPoints: Delay means skills are acquired later than expected; regression means previously acquired skills are lost.

source.raw: Growth, Nutrition & Development — Developmental Assessment.

questions.stem: A child loses previously acquired words and social interaction skills. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
questions.correctAnswerText: Developmental regression requiring prompt assessment
questions.initialExplanation: Loss of previously acquired developmental skills is regression. It is more concerning than an isolated delay and requires evaluation for neurological, metabolic, genetic or other causes.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Correct. Regression is a red flag requiring prompt evaluation.

- A: Incorrect. This resembles some balanced structural rearrangements, not aneuploidy.

- B: Incorrect. A single nucleotide variant is a sequence-level change, not aneuploidy. 
- C: Incorrect. Gene expression is not chromosome number. 
- D: Correct. Aneuploidy involves individual chromosome gain or loss, such as 2n+1 or 2n−1. 
- E: Incorrect. This describes polyploidy.

- A: Incorrect. Erythropoiesis has no role in chromosome segregation. 
- B: Incorrect. A small deletion causes a structural or gene-level abnormality, not classic whole-chromosome trisomy. 
- C: Incorrect. Normal recombination does not itself produce aneuploidy.

- D: Correct. Nondisjunction is the classic mechanism producing aneuploid gametes. 
- E: Incorrect. Protein translation is unrelated to chromosome segregation.

questions.stem: Why does fetal hyperinsulinaemia develop in poorly controlled maternal diabetes?

options.label: A
options.text: Maternal insulin crosses the placenta and directly stimulates the fetal pancreas

options.label: B
options.text: Placental transfer of glucose is completely blocked

options.label: C
options.text: Fetal glucagon is converted into insulin

options.label: D
options.text: The fetal pancreas is unable to detect glucose

options.label: E
options.text: Maternal glucose crosses the placenta, causing fetal hyperglycaemia and stimulation of fetal pancreatic beta cells

questions.correctAnswerText: Maternal glucose crosses the placenta, causing fetal hyperglycaemia and stimulation of fetal pancreatic beta cells
questions.initialExplanation: Maternal glucose crosses the placenta. Fetal hyperglycaemia stimulates pancreatic beta cells, causing hyperinsulinaemia and increased tissue growth and fat deposition.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Incorrect. Maternal insulin does not normally cross the placenta in clinically significant amounts. 
- B: Incorrect. Glucose crosses the placenta; this is central to the mechanism. 
- C: Incorrect. Glucagon is not converted into insulin.

- D: Incorrect. The fetal pancreas responds to the increased glucose concentration. 
- E: Correct. Transplacental glucose drives fetal insulin secretion.

questions.stem: Why is neonatal hypoglycaemia common in IDM after delivery?

options.label: A
options.text: Maternal insulin enters neonatal blood through breast milk immediately after birth

options.label: B
options.text: Persistent fetal hyperinsulinaemia after interruption of maternal glucose supply

options.label: C
options.text: Complete absence of hepatic glycogen in each IDM

options.label: D
options.text: Failure of the kidneys to excrete glucose

questions.correctAnswerText: Persistent fetal hyperinsulinaemia after interruption of maternal glucose supply
questions.initialExplanation: After delivery, placental glucose transfer abruptly ends but neonatal insulin secretion may remain high for a period. This drives glucose into tissues and can cause early neonatal hypoglycaemia.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Incorrect. This is not the mechanism. 
- B: Correct. Persistent hyperinsulinaemia following birth is the key mechanism. 
- C: Incorrect. Hepatic glycogen may be increased due to fetal hyperinsulinaemia. 
- D: Incorrect. Renal glucose handling does not explain the postnatal fall in blood glucose.

- E: Incorrect. Increased glucagon would tend to raise glucose rather than cause the typical pattern.
questions.highYieldPoints: Early feeding and glucose screening are important in at-risk newborns; symptomatic hypoglycaemia needs urgent treatment.

options.label: D
options.text: Chronic fetal hypoxaemia stimulates erythropoietin and erythropoiesis

- A: Incorrect. Hyperinsulinaemia does not directly destroy red cells.

questions.stem: Which early bedside action is particularly important for an at-risk IDM?

options.label: A
options.text: Initiate early feeding and screen glucose according to the neonatal protocol

options.label: B
options.text: Avoid checking glucose if the infant appears well

options.label: D
options.text: Delay feeding until the first glucose test is abnormal

questions.correctAnswerText: Initiate early feeding and screen glucose according to the neonatal protocol

questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Correct. Early feeding and screening are core management measures. 
- B: Incorrect. Hypoglycaemia may be asymptomatic initially. 
- C: Incorrect. Insulin would worsen neonatal hypoglycaemia. 
- D: Incorrect. Early feeding is generally encouraged, rather than delayed. 
- E: Incorrect. Glucose-lowering medication is inappropriate prophylaxis.

questions.stem: Which intervention is appropriate for a symptomatic IDM with significant hypoglycaemia?

options.label: D
options.text: Give an appropriate IV dextrose bolus and infusion with serial glucose monitoring

questions.correctAnswerText: Give an appropriate IV dextrose bolus and infusion with serial glucose monitoring
questions.initialExplanation: Symptomatic neonatal hypoglycaemia requires prompt correction, commonly with IV dextrose followed by an infusion and frequent glucose checks. The standard clinical guidance describes a 10% dextrose bolus and infusion; confirm exact dosing with current neonatal protocol.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Incorrect. Glucose is required to correct hypoglycaemia. 
- B: Incorrect. Antihypertensive therapy does not address the problem. 
- C: Incorrect. Feeding is generally encouraged as soon as safely possible.

- D: Correct. IV dextrose is used in symptomatic cases, alongside monitoring and feeding support. 
- E: Incorrect. Insulin would worsen hypoglycaemia.

questions.stem: Which electrolyte disturbance may occur in IDM during the first 24–72 hours?

options.label: A
options.text: Severe hypernatraemia as an obligatory feature

options.label: B
options.text: No electrolyte abnormalities are associated with IDM

questions.correctAnswerText: Hypocalcaemia
questions.initialExplanation: Hypocalcaemia is a recognized complication in IDM and commonly appears during the first 24–72 hours. The source attributes it to impaired placental calcium transfer, delayed postnatal parathyroid response and reduced mineral stores.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Incorrect. Hypernatraemia is not an obligatory IDM disturbance. 
- B: Incorrect. Several electrolyte and metabolic abnormalities are recognized.

- C: Correct. Hypocalcaemia is a common metabolic complication. 
- D: Incorrect. Hypercalcaemia is not the expected pattern. 
- E: Incorrect. This is not the characteristic universal disturbance.

questions.stem: What is the relationship between hypomagnesaemia and hypocalcaemia in IDM?

options.label: B
options.text: Calcium replacement is not usually required when magnesium is low

options.label: D
options.text: Hypomagnesaemia can contribute to persistent hypocalcaemia

options.label: E
options.text: Magnesium has no relationship to calcium regulation

questions.correctAnswerText: Hypomagnesaemia can contribute to persistent hypocalcaemia
questions.initialExplanation: Magnesium deficiency can impair parathyroid hormone secretion and action, contributing to hypocalcaemia. Both electrolytes may need assessment and correction.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Incorrect. Both disturbances can produce neuromuscular irritability and seizures. 
- B: Incorrect. Treatment depends on clinical severity and measured levels; magnesium should also be corrected when deficient. 
- C: Incorrect. Hypomagnesaemia is not defined by neonatal hyperglycaemia.

- D: Correct. Hypomagnesaemia can make hypocalcaemia difficult to correct. 
- E: Incorrect. Magnesium is important in calcium regulation.

questions.stem: Why are neonatal seizures more likely in the immature brain?

options.label: A
options.text: Neonates have no metabolic causes of seizures

options.label: C
options.text: The immature brain has increased excitability and relatively immature inhibitory neurotransmission

options.label: D
options.text: The newborn brain has complete inhibitory GABA function from birth

options.label: E
options.text: Neonatal neurons cannot generate electrical impulses

questions.correctAnswerText: The immature brain has increased excitability and relatively immature inhibitory neurotransmission
questions.initialExplanation: Immature neuronal ion transport and increased excitatory receptor activity, together with delayed development of inhibitory GABAergic transmission, contribute to increased neonatal brain excitability.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Incorrect. Hypoglycaemia, electrolyte disturbances and metabolic disease are important causes.

- B: Incorrect. NMDA receptor activity is increased in the immature brain, not absent. 
- C: Correct. This describes the developmental neurophysiology outlined. 
- D: Incorrect. GABAergic inhibition is immature, and GABA may have depolarizing effects in the immature brain. 
- E: Incorrect. Neurons generate electrical activity; abnormal synchronized discharges can produce seizures.
questions.highYieldPoints: Neonatal seizures may be subtle and may reflect underlying acute brain injury or systemic/metabolic disease.

questions.stem: Which cause is especially important in the first four days of life?

options.label: A
options.text: Drug withdrawal as the possible cause

options.label: C
options.text: Febrile seizure due to toddler viral illness

questions.correctAnswerText: Hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy
questions.initialExplanation: Hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy is a major early cause of neonatal seizures. Other early causes include acute metabolic disturbances, intracranial haemorrhage, infection and metabolic/genetic disorders.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Incorrect. Drug withdrawal may be relevant in selected contexts, but is not the only or defining early cause. 
- B: Incorrect. Migraine is not a neonatal seizure etiology. 
- C: Incorrect. Febrile seizures are not the typical explanation in the neonatal period. 
- D: Incorrect. Neonatal seizures have a broad acute symptomatic differential.

- E: Correct. HIE is a leading early neonatal seizure cause.

options.label: C

options.label: E
options.text: Repetitive mouthing, eye deviation, bicycling movements or autonomic changes

questions.correctAnswerText: Repetitive mouthing, eye deviation, bicycling movements or autonomic changes

- B: Incorrect. Fever alone is not a seizure manifestation. 
- C: Incorrect. Neonatal seizures often do not resemble generalized tonic-clonic seizures.

options.label: D

options.label: E

- A: Incorrect. Autonomic phenomena may accompany seizures. 
- B: Incorrect. Stereotyped apnea and ocular movements are concerning for seizures.

- C: Incorrect. Eye deviation supports a possible seizure. 
- D: Correct. Suppressibility and stimulus sensitivity favour jitteriness.

questions.stem: What does the P wave represent on an ECG?
questions.correctAnswerText: Atrial depolarization
questions.initialExplanation: The P wave represents atrial depolarization. It is normally a smooth deflection and is generally upright in leads I and II, with a negative P wave in aVR.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Incorrect. Ventricular repolarization is represented by the T wave. 
- B: Incorrect. Ventricular ejection occurs after electrical depolarization and is not itself an ECG wave.

- C: Incorrect. Valve closure is not directly represented by the P wave. 
- D: Incorrect. Ventricular depolarization is represented by the QRS complex. 
- E: Correct. The P wave represents atrial depolarization.
questions.highYieldPoints: A normal P-wave duration is less than 0.12 seconds in the standard clinical guidance; interpret morphology and duration in the pediatric age context.

options.label: A
options.text: Time between two consecutive R waves

options.label: B
options.text: Time from the end of the QRS complex to the end of the T wave

options.label: C
options.text: Time from the start to the end of the QRS complex

options.label: D
options.text: Time from the beginning of the P wave to the beginning of the QRS complex

options.label: E
options.text: Time from the end of the P wave to the end of the T wave

questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Incorrect. This is the RR interval. 
- B: Incorrect. This does not represent the PR interval. 
- C: Incorrect. This describes QRS duration. 
- D: Correct. This is the standard definition of the PR interval. 
- E: Incorrect. The PR interval begins at the onset, not end, of the P wave and ends at QRS onset.
questions.highYieldPoints: Standard reference values include a usual PR interval of 0.12–0.20 seconds; neonatal and pediatric reference values vary with age and heart rate.

questions.stem: Which electrical event is represented by the QRS complex?
questions.correctAnswerText: Ventricular depolarization
questions.initialExplanation: The QRS complex represents ventricular depolarization. Atrial repolarization occurs at approximately the same time but is usually obscured by the QRS complex.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Correct. The QRS complex represents ventricular depolarization. 
- B: Incorrect. Ventricular repolarization is represented by the T wave. 
- C: Incorrect. Atrial depolarization is represented by the P wave. 
- D: Incorrect. SA node automaticity is not represented by the QRS complex.

- E: Incorrect. Atrial repolarization is not separately visible in normal ECGs and is not what the QRS primarily represents.

questions.stem: Which formula is used to calculate the corrected QT interval (QTc)?
questions.correctAnswerText: QT ÷ √RR
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance uses Bazett's formula: QTc = QT divided by the square root of the RR interval. QT correction is important because the QT interval changes with heart rate.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Correct. This is Bazett's formula as presented. 
- B: Incorrect. Multiplication is not the formula. 
- C: Incorrect. PR is not included. 
- D: Incorrect. This reverses the ratio and omits the square root. 
- E: Incorrect. QRS duration and heart rate are not combined in this way.
questions.highYieldPoints: Prolonged QT predisposes to ventricular arrhythmias; check units and the method used when calculating QTc.

- B: Incorrect. A short PR interval and delta wave suggest pre-excitation such as WPW. 
- C: Incorrect. Saw-tooth waves suggest atrial flutter. 
- D: Correct. These are classic hyperkalaemic ECG changes. 
- E: Incorrect. Prominent U waves and ST depression are typical of hypokalaemia.

- D: Incorrect. A sine-wave pattern is a severe hyperkalaemic feature.

questions.stem: Which ECG description is typical of a premature ventricular contraction (PVC)?

options.label: A
options.text: An early, wide QRS complex that differs from the normal complexes

options.label: C
options.text: An early abnormal P wave followed by a narrow QRS

options.label: E
options.text: A normal narrow QRS after each P wave

questions.correctAnswerText: An early, wide QRS complex that differs from the normal complexes
questions.initialExplanation: A PVC is a premature ventricular beat, typically appearing as an early broad QRS complex with morphology different from the normal conducted complexes.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Correct. An early, wide, abnormal QRS is the characteristic appearance. 
- B: Incorrect. This is the pattern of Mobitz I AV block. 
- C: Incorrect. This describes a premature atrial contraction. 
- D: Incorrect. Saw-tooth baseline suggests atrial flutter.

- E: Incorrect. This describes normal sinus conduction.
questions.highYieldPoints: Bigeminy means every second beat is ectopic; trigeminy means every third beat is ectopic.

source.raw: Cardiovascular System — ECG in Pediatrics, pp. 70–72.

questions.stem: Which finding defines first-degree AV block?

options.label: A
options.text: Constant prolongation of the PR interval with each P wave followed by a QRS

options.label: B
options.text: A wide QRS after each premature P wave

options.label: D
options.text: Random failure of AV conduction without PR prolongation

options.label: E
options.text: Progressive PR prolongation with a dropped QRS

questions.correctAnswerText: Constant prolongation of the PR interval with each P wave followed by a QRS
questions.initialExplanation: First-degree AV block is delayed AV conduction, producing a prolonged but constant PR interval. Every atrial impulse is still conducted to the ventricles.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Correct. Prolonged constant PR with 1:1 conduction is first-degree AV block. 
- B: Incorrect. This describes neither first-degree AV block nor its defining feature.

- C: Incorrect. This defines third-degree AV block. 
- D: Incorrect. This is characteristic of Mobitz II second-degree block. 
- E: Incorrect. This describes Mobitz I second-degree block.
questions.highYieldPoints: In first-degree AV block no QRS is dropped; the delay is reflected in the prolonged PR interval.

source.raw: Cardiovascular System — ECG in Pediatrics, pp. 75–76.

questions.stem: Which pattern is characteristic of Mobitz type I second-degree AV block?

options.label: A
options.text: Progressive PR prolongation followed by a non-conducted P wave

options.label: C
options.text: Complete dissociation of P waves and QRS complexes

options.label: D
options.text: Sudden wide QRS without a preceding P wave

options.label: E
options.text: Constant PR interval with most beats conducted

questions.correctAnswerText: Progressive PR prolongation followed by a non-conducted P wave
questions.initialExplanation: Mobitz I (Wenckebach) block shows progressive prolongation of the PR interval until an atrial impulse fails to conduct and a QRS is dropped.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Correct. This is the defining Wenckebach pattern. 
- B: Incorrect. This suggests pre-excitation.

- C: Incorrect. This describes complete heart block. 
- D: Incorrect. This is more consistent with a PVC. 
- E: Incorrect. This is normal conduction or first-degree block if PR is prolonged.
questions.highYieldPoints: Mobitz II is more concerning because dropped beats occur without preceding progressive PR prolongation and may progress to complete block.

source.raw: Cardiovascular System — ECG in Pediatrics, p. 77.

questions.stem: Which finding is typical of third-degree AV block?

options.label: A
options.text: Complete dissociation between atrial and ventricular activity

options.label: B
options.text: most P waves conduct with a prolonged PR interval

options.label: C
options.text: Progressive PR prolongation before a dropped beat

options.label: E
options.text: Sinus tachycardia with a narrow QRS

questions.correctAnswerText: Complete dissociation between atrial and ventricular activity
questions.initialExplanation: Third-degree AV block is complete failure of atrial impulses to conduct to the ventricles, resulting in independent atrial and ventricular rhythms.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Correct. Complete AV dissociation defines third-degree block. 
- B: Incorrect. This is first-degree AV block. 
- C: Incorrect. This is Mobitz I. 
- D: Incorrect. PACs are ectopic atrial beats, not complete AV block.

- E: Incorrect. This is a possible normal sinus rhythm variant depending on age and context.
questions.highYieldPoints: Consider congenital and acquired causes; assess haemodynamic stability and urgent cardiology input.

source.raw: Cardiovascular System — ECG in Pediatrics, p. 78.

questions.stem: Which lead pattern supports right ventricular hypertrophy in a child?

options.label: A
options.text: No QRS voltage in most leads

options.label: B
options.text: Right axis deviation with a dominant R wave in V1

options.label: C
options.text: Short PR interval with no QRS changes

options.label: D
options.text: Left axis deviation with a dominant R wave in V6

options.label: E
options.text: Isolated peaked T waves in each lead

questions.correctAnswerText: Right axis deviation with a dominant R wave in V1
questions.initialExplanation: Common examples include right-axis deviation and a dominant R wave in V1 as features supporting RVH. Pediatric interpretation must account for age-related normal ECG variation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Incorrect. Low voltage has a broad differential and is not diagnostic of RVH. 
- B: Correct. These are key RVH features. 
- C: Incorrect. Pre-excitation is not an RVH criterion.

- D: Incorrect. This pattern is more consistent with LVH. 
- E: Incorrect. Peaked T waves suggest an electrolyte abnormality such as hyperkalaemia.
questions.highYieldPoints: Neonatal and infant ECGs differ from adult ECGs; do not apply adult voltage and axis cut-offs indiscriminately.

source.raw: Cardiovascular System — ECG in Pediatrics, pp. 80–81.

questions.stem: What is a classic ECG pattern of dextrocardia with mirror-image anatomy?

options.label: A
options.text: Positive P, QRS and T in lead I with normal R-wave progression

options.label: C
options.text: Predominantly negative P, QRS and T in lead I with positive QRS in aVR

options.label: D
options.text: Saw-tooth flutter waves in most leads

questions.correctAnswerText: Predominantly negative P, QRS and T in lead I with positive QRS in aVR
questions.initialExplanation: Dextrocardia may produce negative P, QRS and T deflections in lead I, a positive QRS in aVR, right axis deviation and reverse precordial R-wave progression.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Incorrect. This is more consistent with normal cardiac orientation. 
- B: Incorrect. Isolated ST elevation is not the defining dextrocardia pattern. 
- C: Correct. This is the classic pattern listed. 
- D: Incorrect. This describes atrial flutter.

- E: Incorrect. QT prolongation is unrelated to cardiac mirror-image position.
questions.highYieldPoints: Check limb-lead and precordial electrode placement before diagnosing dextrocardia; technical lead reversal can mimic abnormalities.

source.raw: Cardiovascular System — ECG in Pediatrics, p. 58.

questions.stem: What is the classic cardiac silhouette described as a boot-shaped heart?
questions.correctAnswerText: Tetralogy of Fallot
questions.initialExplanation: Tetralogy of Fallot classically produces a boot-shaped cardiac silhouette due to right ventricular hypertrophy and an upturned apex.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Incorrect. TGA is classically associated with an egg-on-a-string appearance. 
- B: Incorrect. Ebstein anomaly may produce a box-shaped silhouette due to marked right atrial enlargement. 
- C: Incorrect. Supracardiac TAPVR may produce a snowman or figure-of-eight appearance. 
- D: Incorrect. Coarctation is associated with the figure-of-three sign and rib notching.

- E: Correct. Boot-shaped heart is associated with TOF.
questions.highYieldPoints: Radiographic shape is a clue, not a definitive diagnosis; correlate with examination and echocardiography.

source.raw: Cardiovascular System — Radiological Approach to Pediatric Cardiovascular Disorders, pp. 23–27 and 36.

questions.stem: Which cardiac silhouette is classically associated with transposition of the great arteries?
questions.correctAnswerText: Egg-on-a-string appearance
questions.initialExplanation: TGA is classically associated with an egg-on-a-string appearance on chest radiography, reflecting the narrow superior mediastinum and characteristic cardiac contour.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Correct. Egg-on-a-string is associated with TGA. 
- B: Incorrect. This suggests TOF. 
- C: Incorrect. Snowman sign suggests supracardiac TAPVR. 
- D: Incorrect. Box-shaped heart is associated with Ebstein anomaly. 
- E: Incorrect. Figure-of-three sign suggests coarctation of the aorta.
questions.highYieldPoints: TGA is a cyanotic congenital heart disease; the chest radiograph should not delay urgent clinical assessment and echocardiography.

source.raw: Cardiovascular System — Radiological Approach to Pediatric Cardiovascular Disorders, pp. 23–25.

questions.stem: Which radiographic appearance is classically associated with supracardiac TAPVR?
questions.correctAnswerText: Snowman or figure-of-eight sign
questions.initialExplanation: Supracardiac total anomalous pulmonary venous return may create a snowman or figure-of-eight cardiac silhouette.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Incorrect. Egg-on-a-string suggests TGA. 
- B: Incorrect. Boot-shaped heart suggests TOF. 
- C: Incorrect. Air bronchograms are a lung radiographic sign, not a cardiac silhouette.

- D: Correct. This is the classic appearance. 
- E: Incorrect. Figure-of-three suggests coarctation.
questions.highYieldPoints: The sign is dependent on anatomy and age; echocardiography confirms the diagnosis.

source.raw: Cardiovascular System — Radiological Approach to Pediatric Cardiovascular Disorders, pp. 23–27.

questions.stem: What does pulmonary plethora on a pediatric chest radiograph suggest?

options.label: A
options.text: Reduced pulmonary blood flow from a right-to-left shunt

options.label: C
options.text: Increased pulmonary vascularity, commonly due to a left-to-right shunt

options.label: E
options.text: Complete absence of pulmonary blood flow

questions.correctAnswerText: Increased pulmonary vascularity, commonly due to a left-to-right shunt
questions.initialExplanation: Pulmonary plethora reflects increased pulmonary blood flow and can occur with left-to-right shunts such as VSD, ASD or PDA.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Incorrect. Reduced pulmonary blood flow (oligemia) is more typical of TOF and right-to-left shunting. 
- B: Incorrect. Pneumothorax causes pleural air and absent peripheral lung markings. 
- C: Correct. Increased vascular markings suggest increased pulmonary blood flow. 
- D: Incorrect. Airway obstruction may produce hyperinflation or collapse, not generalized pulmonary plethora.

- E: Incorrect. Plethora indicates increased rather than absent flow.
questions.highYieldPoints: Plethora = increased pulmonary vascularity; oligemia = reduced pulmonary vascularity. Interpret with cardiac silhouette and clinical cyanosis.

source.raw: Cardiovascular System — Radiological Approach to Pediatric Cardiovascular Disorders, pp. 4 and 28–30.

questions.stem: What is the most appropriate first-line definitive imaging modality when structural congenital heart disease is suspected?
questions.correctAnswerText: Echocardiography
questions.initialExplanation: Echocardiography is the gold-standard investigation for definitive diagnosis of many pediatric structural cardiac disorders. It provides information on anatomy, chamber size, function and blood flow.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Incorrect. CT head is unrelated. 
- B: Incorrect. It does not assess cardiac structure adequately. 
- C: Incorrect. DMSA evaluates renal cortical uptake and scarring. 
- D: Incorrect. Bone scintigraphy is not a cardiac structural test.

- E: Correct. Echo is the first-line definitive cardiac imaging modality described.
questions.highYieldPoints: CXR is a useful screening tool; echo is definitive for many defects; CT/MRI are selected for complex anatomy or functional assessment.

source.raw: Cardiovascular System — Radiological Approach to Pediatric Cardiovascular Disorders, pp. 33–37.

questions.stem: What is a major limitation of an AP portable chest radiograph when assessing heart size?

options.label: A
options.text: It magnifies the cardiac silhouette and can falsely suggest cardiomegaly

questions.correctAnswerText: It magnifies the cardiac silhouette and can falsely suggest cardiomegaly
questions.initialExplanation: In AP portable films, the heart is farther from the detector and appears magnified. This can falsely increase the cardiothoracic ratio.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Correct. This is the key limitation. 
- B: Incorrect. Lung fields remain visible, though image quality may be limited. 
- C: Incorrect. Plain radiographs do not show detailed valve anatomy.

- D: Incorrect. AP projection tends to magnify, not reduce, apparent heart size. 
- E: Incorrect. Chest radiography uses ionizing radiation.
questions.highYieldPoints: Consider projection, inspiration and rotation before calling cardiomegaly; an AP film in a crying infant may be misleading.

source.raw: Cardiovascular System — Radiological Approach to Pediatric Cardiovascular Disorders, pp. 9–15.

questions.stem: What is the cardiothoracic ratio (CTR)?

options.label: A
options.text: Heart rate divided by respiratory rate

options.label: B
options.text: Maximum transverse cardiac diameter divided by maximum internal thoracic diameter

options.label: C
options.text: Pulmonary artery diameter divided by aortic diameter

options.label: D
options.text: Cardiac output divided by body surface area

options.label: E
options.text: Left ventricular volume divided by right ventricular volume

questions.correctAnswerText: Maximum transverse cardiac diameter divided by maximum internal thoracic diameter
questions.initialExplanation: CTR is calculated by dividing the sum of the right and left maximum cardiac distances from the midline by the maximum internal thoracic width.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Incorrect. This is not an imaging ratio. 
- B: Correct. This is the radiographic definition. 
- C: Incorrect. This is unrelated to CTR. 
- D: Incorrect. Cardiac index is cardiac output relative to body surface area.

- E: Incorrect. Ventricular volume ratio is not CTR.
questions.highYieldPoints: Standard guidance gives up to 60% as potentially normal in neonates/infants and less than 50% in older children on an appropriate PA film; projection affects interpretation.

source.raw: Cardiovascular System — Radiological Approach to Pediatric Cardiovascular Disorders, pp. 19–20.

questions.stem: What is the definition of pediatric heart failure?

options.label: A
options.text: Inability of the heart to pump blood at a rate adequate for metabolic needs and tissue oxygen delivery

options.label: C
options.text: A heart rate below 60 beats/min in children in routine care

options.label: D
options.text: A normal cardiac output with no symptoms

questions.correctAnswerText: Inability of the heart to pump blood at a rate adequate for metabolic needs and tissue oxygen delivery
questions.initialExplanation: Pediatric heart failure is a clinical syndrome in which cardiac output is inadequate for metabolic demands, or is maintained only at the expense of elevated filling pressures.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Correct. This is standard guidance definition. 
- B: Incorrect. A murmur may be innocent or pathological and does not itself define heart failure. 
- C: Incorrect. Bradycardia is not the defining feature. 
- D: Incorrect. This does not represent heart failure.

- E: Incorrect. Hypertension may contribute to heart failure but is not the definition.
questions.highYieldPoints: Pediatric presentation is age-dependent; infants may present with poor feeding, sweating and failure to thrive rather than typical adult symptoms.

source.raw: Cardiovascular System — Approach to a Child with Heart Failure, pp. 3–4.

questions.stem: Which haemodynamic abnormality is described as the most common cause of heart failure in children?
questions.correctAnswerText: Volume overload
questions.initialExplanation: Recognized features include volume overload as the most common cause of pediatric heart failure. Left-to-right shunts such as VSD and PDA can increase pulmonary flow and preload.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Incorrect. Coronary vasospasm is not the commonest pediatric mechanism described. 
- B: Incorrect. Reduced systemic vascular resistance is not the defining cause. 
- C: Incorrect. Severe reduction in preload may reduce output but is not the commonest cause. 
- D: Correct. Volume overload is explicitly identified as the commonest mechanism. 
- E: Incorrect. Afterload excess may cause heart failure in selected obstructive lesions, but not in every case.
questions.highYieldPoints: Distinguish preload (ventricular filling/volume) from afterload (resistance against which the ventricle ejects).

source.raw: Cardiovascular System — Approach to a Child with Heart Failure, pp. 4–5.

questions.stem: Which clinical presentation is most typical of heart failure in an infant?

options.label: D
options.text: Poor feeding, tachypnoea, diaphoresis during feeds and failure to thrive

questions.correctAnswerText: Poor feeding, tachypnoea, diaphoresis during feeds and failure to thrive
questions.initialExplanation: Infants may develop tachypnoea, sweating and fatigue with feeding, poor intake and failure to thrive. Older children more often describe exertional dyspnoea and fatigue.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Incorrect. Hearing loss is not a typical heart failure presentation. 
- B: Incorrect. Joint or limb pain does not define infant heart failure. 
- C: Incorrect. Haematuria suggests urinary tract or renal disease.

- D: Correct. These are classic infant presentations. 
- E: Incorrect. This suggests a possible diabetes presentation.
questions.highYieldPoints: Feeding is an exertional activity for infants; observe feeding effort, respiratory rate and sweating.

source.raw: Cardiovascular System — Approach to a Child with Heart Failure, p. 8.

questions.stem: Which finding is more suggestive of right-sided heart failure?
questions.correctAnswerText: Hepatomegaly and peripheral oedema
questions.initialExplanation: Systemic venous congestion from right-sided failure may cause hepatomegaly, oedema and distended neck veins. Left-sided failure more commonly causes pulmonary venous congestion and respiratory symptoms.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Incorrect. Wheeze may occur in pulmonary congestion but is not a specific right-sided sign. 
- B: Incorrect. Haematuria is a renal/urinary finding.

- C: Incorrect. Epistaxis is not a sign of right-sided heart failure. 
- D: Incorrect. Hemarthrosis suggests a bleeding disorder. 
- E: Correct. These findings are characteristic of systemic venous congestion.
questions.highYieldPoints: Left-sided failure → pulmonary congestion; right-sided failure → systemic venous congestion; both may coexist.

source.raw: Cardiovascular System — Approach to a Child with Heart Failure, p. 8.

questions.stem: Which biomarker is released in response to myocardial pressure or volume stress and can help support the diagnosis of heart failure?
questions.correctAnswerText: BNP or NT-proBNP
questions.initialExplanation: BNP and NT-proBNP are released in response to cardiac wall stress. Low levels have a high negative predictive value in the appropriate clinical setting, while elevated levels may support diagnosis and help assess severity.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Incorrect. Bilirubin may be abnormal in liver disease or congestion but is not the specific cardiac biomarker.

- B: Incorrect. Troponin is used to assess myocardial injury and is not the biomarker highlighted for general HF support. 
- C: Incorrect. Amylase is a pancreatic enzyme. 
- D: Correct. These are the cardiac biomarkers described. 
- E: Incorrect. Urinary ketones are relevant to ketosis, not heart failure diagnosis.
questions.highYieldPoints: BNP/NT-proBNP support the clinical assessment; neither should replace history, examination and echocardiography.

source.raw: Cardiovascular System — Approach to a Child with Heart Failure, pp. 12–13.

questions.stem: Which treatment is considered a cornerstone for reducing congestion in pediatric heart failure?

options.label: C
options.text: Antiplatelet therapy in children in routine care

questions.correctAnswerText: Diuretics
questions.initialExplanation: Diuretics reduce preload and relieve fluid congestion. Treatment should be directed at the underlying etiology and may also include afterload reduction or inotropic support when indicated.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Incorrect. Antituberculous treatment is used for tuberculosis, not general heart failure. 
- B: Incorrect. Insulin is not a routine heart failure treatment. 
- C: Incorrect. Antiplatelet therapy is not universal heart failure treatment.

- D: Correct. Diuretics are the cornerstone for treating congestion in the standard clinical guidance. 
- E: Incorrect. Anticonvulsants do not treat cardiac congestion.
questions.highYieldPoints: Common examples include diuretics, inotropes and afterload-reducing agents; select therapy according to haemodynamics and cause.

source.raw: Cardiovascular System — Approach to a Child with Heart Failure, p. 14.

questions.stem: What is the most appropriate interpretation of dense homogeneous lobar consolidation with air bronchograms on a chest radiograph?

options.label: D
options.text: Diagnostic proof of a viral organism

options.label: E
options.text: A pattern that favours lobar pneumonia, commonly bacterial in the appropriate clinical context

questions.correctAnswerText: A pattern that favours lobar pneumonia, commonly bacterial in the appropriate clinical context
questions.initialExplanation: Lobar consolidation occurs when alveoli fill with inflammatory exudate and is classically associated with bacterial pneumonia, particularly pneumococcal disease. Air bronchograms may be visible because air-filled bronchi are outlined by opaque alveoli.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Incorrect. Pneumothorax is suggested by a pleural line and absent peripheral lung markings.

- B: Incorrect. Pulmonary embolism is not diagnosed by this pattern. 
- C: Incorrect. Dense lobar opacity is abnormal. 
- D: Incorrect. Radiographic patterns overlap; consolidation does not prove a viral cause. 
- E: Correct. This is the classic pattern, although it is not organism-specific.
questions.highYieldPoints: Describe the pattern and distribution before suggesting etiology; correlate with clinical and microbiological findings.

source.raw: Respiratory System & Chest Imaging — Pediatric Chest Imaging, pp. 12–17.

questions.stem: What does ground-glass opacity (GGO) mean on chest CT?

options.label: A
options.text: Complete replacement of the lung by air

options.label: B
options.text: A pleural line with no peripheral markings

options.label: C
options.text: A cavity containing an air-fluid level

options.label: D
options.text: Increased lung attenuation through which vessels and bronchial walls remain visible

options.label: E
options.text: A normal finding in most children

questions.correctAnswerText: Increased lung attenuation through which vessels and bronchial walls remain visible
questions.initialExplanation: GGO is increased pulmonary attenuation that does not completely obscure underlying vessels and bronchial walls. It may occur in viral infection but is nonspecific.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Incorrect. This describes excessive lucency rather than GGO. 
- B: Incorrect. This is a sign of pneumothorax. 
- C: Incorrect. This describes a cavity or abscess. 
- D: Correct. This is the radiological definition of GGO. 
- E: Incorrect. GGO is an abnormal imaging finding that requires context.
questions.highYieldPoints: GGO occurs in viral and bacterial infection, pulmonary oedema, haemorrhage and other conditions; it is not organism-specific.

source.raw: Respiratory System & Chest Imaging — Pediatric Chest Imaging, pp. 6–7 and 19–20.

questions.stem: What does a tree-in-bud pattern most strongly suggest?

options.label: D
options.text: Small-airway or bronchiolar inflammation with impacted/inflamed terminal airways

options.label: E
options.text: A normal variant in each infant

questions.correctAnswerText: Small-airway or bronchiolar inflammation with impacted/inflamed terminal airways
questions.initialExplanation: Tree-in-bud opacities represent branching centrilobular abnormalities associated with small-airway inflammation or impaction, including infectious bronchiolitis and tuberculosis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Incorrect. This is not a cardiac radiographic pattern. 
- B: Incorrect. Lung agenesis is a different structural abnormality. 
- C: Incorrect. Pleural effusion is fluid in the pleural space. 
- D: Correct. This is the pathophysiological meaning of the pattern. 
- E: Incorrect. Tree-in-bud is not a universal normal finding.
questions.highYieldPoints: Tree-in-bud suggests bronchiolar disease but does not identify a specific organism.

source.raw: Respiratory System & Chest Imaging — Pediatric Chest Imaging, p. 8.

questions.stem: Which radiographic appearance is more typical of viral lower respiratory tract infection/bronchiolitis?

options.label: A
options.text: A widened mediastinum caused by a thymic sail sign

options.label: B
options.text: A solitary dense lobar opacity in each case

questions.correctAnswerText: Hyperinflation with peribronchial thickening
questions.initialExplanation: Viral respiratory infection, particularly RSV bronchiolitis, may cause hyperinflation, peribronchial cuffing and bilateral interstitial or patchy opacities.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Incorrect. The thymic sail sign is a normal thymic contour in infants, not a viral lung pattern.

- B: Incorrect. Lobar consolidation may occur in bacterial pneumonia, but neither pattern is absolute. 
- C: Correct. These are common viral/bronchiolitic radiographic features. 
- D: Incorrect. Boot-shaped heart suggests TOF. 
- E: Incorrect. Pneumoperitoneum is a finding below the diaphragm.
questions.highYieldPoints: A normal chest radiograph does not exclude viral pneumonia; radiographic findings overlap between pathogens.
