questions.stem: What is the most appropriate indication for chest CT in a child with pneumonia?

options.label: A
options.text: Suspected complication such as abscess, necrosis or empyema, or persistent deterioration/non-resolution

options.label: C
options.text: Routine screening after each antibiotic course

options.label: D
options.text: To identify the pathogen with certainty in typical presentations

questions.correctAnswerText: Suspected complication such as abscess, necrosis or empyema, or persistent deterioration/non-resolution
questions.initialExplanation: CT is more sensitive than chest radiography for subtle parenchymal disease and complications. It is reserved for selected cases, such as suspected abscess, necrotizing pneumonia, empyema, atypical disease or failure to improve.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Correct. These are recognized indications. 
- B: Incorrect. Mild symptoms alone do not justify CT. 
- C: Incorrect. Routine CT follow-up exposes children to unnecessary radiation. 
- D: Incorrect. Imaging cannot reliably identify a specific organism.

- E: Incorrect. CT is not routinely indicated for uncomplicated pneumonia.
questions.highYieldPoints: Ultrasound is often useful for pleural fluid assessment; contrast CT can characterize pleural infection and abscess.

source.raw: Respiratory System & Chest Imaging — Pediatric Chest Imaging, pp. 4–5 and 23–27.

questions.stem: Which finding best distinguishes atelectasis from uncomplicated consolidation on a chest radiograph?

options.label: C
options.text: Volume loss with fissural displacement and crowding of bronchovascular structures

questions.correctAnswerText: Volume loss with fissural displacement and crowding of bronchovascular structures
questions.initialExplanation: Atelectasis is associated with volume loss, displacement of fissures and crowding of structures toward the collapsed region. Consolidation may be dense without significant volume loss.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Incorrect. Air bronchograms can occur in both consolidation and other alveolar processes. 
- B: Incorrect. Pleural fluid does not itself distinguish atelectasis from consolidation. 
- C: Correct. Volume loss is a key discriminating feature. 
- D: Incorrect. CTR is a cardiac measurement.

- E: Incorrect. GGO is nonspecific.
questions.highYieldPoints: Look for volume change and displacement when differentiating collapse from air-space filling.

source.raw: Respiratory System & Chest Imaging — Pediatric Chest Imaging, p. 25.

questions.stem: Why may a chest radiograph fail to show an aspirated peanut in a young child?

options.label: A
options.text: Plain radiography detects metallic objects in typical presentations

options.label: B
options.text: The lungs are not visible on pediatric radiographs

options.label: C
options.text: Most food foreign bodies are radiolucent

options.label: D
options.text: most peanuts dissolve immediately in the airway

options.label: E
options.text: Foreign bodies are typically located below the diaphragm

questions.correctAnswerText: Most food foreign bodies are radiolucent
questions.initialExplanation: Most food foreign bodies, including peanuts, are radiolucent and may not be directly visualized on plain radiographs. Indirect signs of obstruction are often more useful.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Incorrect. Many non-metallic objects are not visible, but not only metallic foreign bodies can be detected.

- B: Incorrect. The lungs remain visible; the foreign body itself may not. 
- C: Correct. Radiolucency explains why the object may not be seen. 
- D: Incorrect. A retained peanut can obstruct the airway. 
- E: Incorrect. Aspirated objects enter the airway, not the abdomen.
questions.highYieldPoints: A normal chest radiograph does not exclude foreign body aspiration when history and examination are convincing.

source.raw: Respiratory System & Chest Imaging — Foreign Body Aspiration in Children, pp. 28–33.

questions.stem: Why is the right main bronchus a common site for an aspirated foreign body?

options.label: A
options.text: The left lung has no bronchi

options.label: B
options.text: The epiglottis directs most objects into the right lung

options.label: C
options.text: The right main bronchus is the airway open at birth

options.label: D
options.text: It has a relatively more direct course from the trachea

options.label: E
options.text: It is longer and narrower than each other airway

questions.correctAnswerText: It has a relatively more direct course from the trachea
questions.initialExplanation: The right main bronchus is often more vertical and aligned with the trachea, making it a common site for aspirated objects.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Incorrect. The left lung has a normal bronchial tree. 
- B: Incorrect. The epiglottis protects the airway and does not selectively direct objects to the right lung.

- C: Incorrect. Both main bronchi are patent at birth. 
- D: Correct. The anatomical orientation explains the tendency. 
- E: Incorrect. The right main bronchus is not defined by being longer and narrower.
questions.highYieldPoints: The exact site also depends on position, age and object size; the right side is common, not exclusive.

questions.stem: What is the ball-valve mechanism in partial bronchial foreign-body obstruction?

options.label: A
options.text: The affected lung collapses immediately in each case

options.label: B
options.text: Air enters during inspiration but is trapped during expiration

options.label: C
options.text: The pleural space fills with fluid

options.label: D

options.label: E

questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Incorrect. Glycosuria alone does not establish DKA.

- B: Correct. All three components are required for the syndrome. 
- C: Incorrect. DKA causes hyperglycaemia, ketosis and acidosis. 
- D: Incorrect. Hypercalcaemia is not part of the diagnostic triad. 
- E: Incorrect. This does not fit the biochemical definition.

questions.stem: When should IV insulin infusion generally be started in pediatric DKA?

options.label: E
options.text: After initial fluid therapy has been running for at least one hour

questions.correctAnswerText: After initial fluid therapy has been running for at least one hour
questions.initialExplanation: An important point is fluid resuscitation first and delaying insulin until IV fluids have been running for at least one hour. Insulin suppresses ketogenesis and corrects acidosis.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Incorrect. Insulin is required to resolve ketosis and acidosis; it is not delayed until resolution. 
- B: Incorrect. Bicarbonate is rarely indicated in pediatric DKA. 
- C: Incorrect. Insulin is started while glucose is elevated, with glucose added to fluids as glucose falls.

- D: Incorrect. Starting insulin before initial fluids may increase risk and is contrary to standard guidance sequence. 
- E: Correct. This is the timing stated in the clinical guidance.

questions.stem: Why is insulin continued even after blood glucose falls during DKA treatment?

options.label: C
options.text: To prevent potassium from entering cells

options.label: D
options.text: To suppress ketogenesis and allow acidosis to resolve

questions.correctAnswerText: To suppress ketogenesis and allow acidosis to resolve
questions.initialExplanation: Insulin must continue to suppress lipolysis and ketone production until ketoacidosis resolves. Dextrose is added to IV fluids as glucose falls to prevent hypoglycaemia while insulin continues.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Incorrect. Hyperglycaemia is not the treatment goal. 
- B: Incorrect. Insulin is not a direct treatment for cerebral oedema.

- C: Incorrect. Insulin promotes intracellular potassium movement and can lower serum potassium. 
- D: Correct. The aim is resolution of ketosis and acidosis, not simply normalization of glucose. 
- E: Incorrect. Osmotic diuresis is a consequence of hyperglycaemia, not the therapeutic aim.
questions.highYieldPoints: Do not reduce the insulin infusion solely because glucose normalizes if ketoacidosis persists; add glucose and follow the DKA protocol.

- A: Incorrect. Otitis media is unrelated to DKA treatment complications. 
- B: Correct. This is the major neurological emergency in DKA. 
- C: Incorrect. Sinusitis is not a DKA complication.

- D: Incorrect. Appendicitis is a differential for abdominal pain, not the treatment complication. 
- E: Incorrect. Cataract is not the acute feared complication.

- D: Incorrect. Proteinuria may indicate kidney damage but does not alone define AKI.

questions.stem: Which group correctly classifies the major anatomical categories of AKI?
questions.correctAnswerText: Pre-renal, intrinsic renal and post-renal
questions.initialExplanation: AKI is classified according to the main site or mechanism of the initial insult: reduced renal perfusion (pre-renal), intrinsic renal injury, or obstruction to urine outflow (post-renal).
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Incorrect. These are broad disease categories, not the AKI classification.

- B: Correct. This is the standard anatomical classification. 
- C: Incorrect. Time course alone does not classify the anatomical cause. 
- D: Incorrect. Hepatic and pulmonary categories do not classify AKI. 
- E: Incorrect. These are possible etiologies but do not form the principal anatomical classification.

questions.stem: Which clinical setting most strongly suggests pre-renal AKI?

options.label: B
options.text: Acute glomerulonephritis with red cell casts

options.label: E
options.text: Severe dehydration after prolonged vomiting and diarrhoea

questions.initialExplanation: Pre-renal AKI results from reduced renal perfusion, commonly due to hypovolaemia, haemorrhage, low cardiac output or systemic vasodilation.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Incorrect. Bilateral obstruction causes post-renal AKI. 
- B: Incorrect. Glomerulonephritis is an intrinsic renal cause. 
- C: Incorrect. Cortical necrosis is intrinsic renal injury.

- D: Incorrect. Interstitial nephritis is intrinsic renal injury. 
- E: Correct. Gastrointestinal fluid loss causes hypovolaemia and reduced renal perfusion.

questions.stem: Which medication exposure should raise concern for nephrotoxic tubular injury?

options.label: C

questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Incorrect. Topical emollients are not a usual cause of tubular injury. 
- B: Correct. Aminoglycosides are a classic nephrotoxic exposure. 
- C: Incorrect. Appropriate vitamin D dosing is not a common cause of AKI. 
- D: Incorrect. Oral rehydration solution is used to replace fluid and electrolytes. 
- E: Incorrect. Isotonic saline is used for volume replacement when clinically indicated.

questions.stem: Which condition is a classic post-renal cause of AKI in a male infant?

questions.stem: Which urine index pattern favours pre-renal azotaemia over acute tubular necrosis (ATN)?

options.label: D
options.text: Urine osmolality below 300 mOsm/kg in each case

options.label: E
options.text: Urine sodium above 40 mmol/L with dilute urine

questions.correctAnswerText: Urine sodium below 15–20 mmol/L and concentrated urine
questions.initialExplanation: In pre-renal states, intact tubules conserve sodium and water, producing low urine sodium and concentrated urine. ATN impairs tubular reabsorption, so urine sodium rises and urine becomes less concentrated.

- A: Incorrect. Low specific gravity suggests poor concentration, often with tubular injury.

- B: Correct. This is the expected pre-renal pattern.

- A: Incorrect. This is unrelated to FeNa.

- C: Incorrect. This does not account for serum concentration or creatinine. 
- D: Correct. This is the formula shown. 
- E: Incorrect. It reverses and misplaces the variables.

questions.stem: Why can serum creatinine be an imperfect early marker of AKI?

options.label: A
options.text: It is typically elevated before urine output changes

options.label: B
options.text: It measures renal function instantaneously in most situations

options.label: C
options.text: It is independent of muscle mass and nutritional status

options.label: D
options.text: It is produced by the kidneys

options.label: E
options.text: It may rise after GFR has already fallen and is influenced by age and muscle mass

questions.correctAnswerText: It may rise after GFR has already fallen and is influenced by age and muscle mass
questions.initialExplanation: Serum creatinine is affected by age, sex, muscle mass, nutrition and hydration. It also lags behind acute changes in GFR because it requires time to accumulate.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Incorrect. Oliguria may occur before a significant creatinine rise.

- B: Incorrect. It is not an instantaneous measure in non-steady-state AKI. 
- C: Incorrect. Creatinine is influenced by muscle mass and other factors. 
- D: Incorrect. Creatinine is generated mainly from muscle creatine metabolism and excreted by the kidneys.

options.label: C
options.text: Persistent severe hyperkalaemia despite medical treatment

options.label: D
options.text: Normal urine output with normal electrolytes

- B: Incorrect. Microscopic haematuria alone is not an indication for dialysis.

- D: Incorrect. There is no indication in this description.

questions.stem: Which definition of CKD is used?

options.text: Any renal stone, regardless of kidney function or duration

options.label: D

options.label: E

questions.correctAnswerText: Kidney damage or reduced GFR below 60 mL/min/1.73 m² persisting for at least three months
questions.initialExplanation: CKD is defined by kidney damage (such as abnormal urinalysis or structural abnormalities) or GFR below 60 mL/min/1.73 m² for at least three months.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Incorrect. Fever and dysuria suggest infection. 
- B: Incorrect. A stone alone does not establish CKD without chronic kidney damage or functional impairment.

- C: Incorrect. Oliguria for one day does not establish chronic kidney disease. 
- D: Incorrect. A transient rise may represent AKI, not CKD. 
- E: Correct. This reflects the chronicity criterion described.

questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Correct. This is stage 3. 
- B: Incorrect. This is stage 4. 
- C: Incorrect. This is stage 2 table. 
- D: Incorrect. This is not the stage 3 range.

- E: Incorrect. This is the preserved GFR range used for stage 1 when damage is present.

questions.stem: Which formula is used to estimate GFR in children?

options.label: B
options.text: Schwartz formula: k × height (cm) ÷ serum creatinine

options.label: D
options.text: Cockcroft–Gault formula using weight and age

questions.correctAnswerText: Schwartz formula: k × height (cm) ÷ serum creatinine
questions.initialExplanation: Standard guidance uses the Schwartz formula, eGFR = k × height in centimetres divided by serum creatinine. The constant k varies according to age, sex and developmental stage.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Incorrect. Potassium and urine output are not used in the equation.

- B: Correct. This is the pediatric Schwartz formula. 
- C: Incorrect. This is not a validated eGFR equation. 
- D: Incorrect. Cockcroft–Gault is not the formula presented for children. 
- E: Incorrect. Sodium does not appear in the formula.

options.label: B
options.text: Posterior urethral valves and congenital obstructive uropathy

questions.stem: Which dietary principle is important in pediatric CKD?

options.text: Individualize protein, sodium, potassium, phosphate, fluid and caloric intake according to growth and biochemical status

options.text: Give unlimited potassium regardless of serum level

options.label: E
options.text: Restrict calories in children in routine care

questions.correctAnswerText: Individualize protein, sodium, potassium, phosphate, fluid and caloric intake according to growth and biochemical status
questions.initialExplanation: Nutritional management must balance renal restrictions with the child's need for growth. Protein, sodium, potassium, phosphate and fluid adjustments depend on the stage of CKD, laboratory results and clinical state.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Incorrect. Fluid balance is a core part of CKD management.

- B: Correct. Individualized nutritional support is essential. 
- C: Incorrect. Potassium intake may need restriction when hyperkalaemia is present. 
- D: Incorrect. Protein restriction should not be excessive and must preserve growth. 
- E: Incorrect. Adequate caloric intake is important to prevent malnutrition.

questions.stem: Which is a major long-term treatment option for a child with end-stage renal disease?

options.label: A

options.label: C
options.text: Repeated courses of oral antibiotics alone

questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Incorrect. Insulin is required only for coexisting diabetes. 
- B: Incorrect. Bronchodilators do not treat ESRD. 
- C: Incorrect. Antibiotics do not replace renal function. 
- D: Incorrect. Fluid restriction alone cannot replace kidney function.

- A: Incorrect. Proteinuria is a separate urinary finding.

questions.correctAnswerText: Onset before 16 years, arthritis lasting at least six weeks and exclusion of other causes
questions.initialExplanation: JIA is arthritis beginning before age 16, lasting at least six weeks, with other causes of chronic arthritis excluded. Arthritis is defined by swelling/effusion or a combination of restricted movement, tenderness/pain on motion and increased heat.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Incorrect. Two days of arthralgia does not meet the chronicity criterion. 
- B: Incorrect. Traumatic swelling is not JIA and needs an alternative explanation.

- C: Correct. This is the core diagnostic framework. 
- D: Incorrect. Fever and joint pain alone do not establish JIA. 
- E: Incorrect. Most JIA patients are RF negative; RF is used for classification and prognosis in selected cases.

questions.stem: How is polyarticular JIA defined by the number of involved joints during the first six months?

options.label: E
options.text: Arthritis with fever but no joint inflammation

- B: Incorrect. Two joints remain below the polyarticular threshold. 
- C: Correct. This is the threshold used. 
- D: Incorrect. A single joint is monoarthritis, not polyarthritis. 
- E: Incorrect. Systemic JIA has systemic features, but arthritis remains part of the diagnosis.
questions.highYieldPoints: Classification is based on the number and pattern of joints in the first six months, not simply the total number ever affected.

questions.stem: Which is the most common JIA subtype in the standard clinical guidance?

questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Incorrect. Systemic JIA is less common.

questions.correctAnswerText: Quotidian high-spiking fever with an evanescent salmon-pink rash

- A: Incorrect. This may suggest a haematological disorder.

- D: Incorrect. RF-positive polyarthritis often resembles adult rheumatoid arthritis.

questions.stem: Which is the most appropriate immediate management of suspected septic arthritis in a febrile, non-weight-bearing child?

questions.correctAnswerText: Urgent orthopedic assessment, joint aspiration/drainage and prompt IV antibiotics after appropriate cultures
questions.initialExplanation: Septic arthritis is an orthopedic emergency because bacterial infection can rapidly damage cartilage. Management includes urgent drainage/aspiration and empiric IV antibiotics, adjusted to culture results.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Incorrect. Physiotherapy cannot replace source control and antimicrobial treatment. 
- B: Incorrect. NSAIDs alone do not treat bacterial infection. 
- C: Incorrect. Steroid injection is contraindicated until septic arthritis has been excluded.

- D: Incorrect. Delayed treatment risks irreversible joint damage. 
- E: Correct. This is the urgent treatment pathway.
questions.highYieldPoints: Obtain blood cultures when feasible, but do not delay emergency antibiotics in an unstable child.

- B: Correct. This is the typical benign pattern. 
- C: Incorrect. Fever and pseudoparalysis in an infant are concerning for infection. 
- D: Incorrect. Purulent fluid and high inflammatory markers support septic arthritis.

questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Incorrect. This suggests toddler's fracture. 
- B: Correct. This is the characteristic age and presentation. 
- C: Incorrect. This suggests septic arthritis or osteomyelitis. 
- D: Incorrect. This is not the typical presentation.

- B: Correct. This is the classic risk profile. 
- C: Incorrect. This raises concern for infection, not SCFE. 
- D: Incorrect. This is a typical growing-pains pattern.

questions.highYieldPoints: SUFE is an orthopedic emergency; avoid weight-bearing and arrange urgent orthopedic referral and appropriate imaging.

questions.stem: Which gait abnormality indicates hip abductor weakness?

questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Incorrect. Antalgic gait shortens stance time on the painful limb. 
- B: Correct. This is the classic Trendelenburg sign. 
- C: Incorrect. Scissor gait is associated with spasticity and adductor overactivity. 
- D: Incorrect. Steppage gait compensates for foot drop. 
- E: Incorrect. Ataxic gait reflects impaired coordination and balance.
questions.highYieldPoints: Trendelenburg gait can occur with Perthes disease, SUFE, DDH, hip JIA and neuromuscular disease.

- A: Incorrect. Persistent restricted hip movement suggests structural or inflammatory pathology.

- C: Incorrect. This suggests inflammatory joint disease. 
- D: Correct. This is the typical pattern.

questions.stem: What is the predominant route of HIV acquisition in children?
questions.correctAnswerText: Mother-to-child transmission
questions.initialExplanation: Recognized features include vertical transmission from mother to child during pregnancy, delivery or breastfeeding as the predominant route of pediatric HIV acquisition.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Incorrect. HIV is not spread by ordinary social contact. 
- B: Incorrect. HIV is not transmitted by mosquitoes. 
- C: Correct. MTCT accounts for the vast majority of pediatric infections in the clinical guidance. 
- D: Incorrect. Intact skin contact does not transmit HIV.

- E: Incorrect. Sharing food or utensils does not transmit HIV.
questions.highYieldPoints: Effective maternal ART, appropriate infant prophylaxis, testing and supported feeding decisions greatly reduce vertical transmission.

questions.stem: Which immune cell is the principal target of HIV?
questions.correctAnswerText: CD4-positive T lymphocyte
questions.initialExplanation: HIV binds to CD4 and co-receptors such as CCR5 or CXCR4, enters susceptible cells and progressively depletes CD4 T lymphocytes, causing immunodeficiency.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Incorrect. Platelets are not the principal target. 
- B: Incorrect. Renal tubular cells are not the primary target.

- C: Correct. CD4 T cells are the primary immune target described. 
- D: Incorrect. Mature red cells do not support HIV replication. 
- E: Incorrect. Other immune cells may be involved, but CD4 T cells are central.
questions.highYieldPoints: Progressive CD4 depletion increases susceptibility to opportunistic infections and certain malignancies.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly describes the HIV replication cycle?

options.label: A
options.text: Budding, antibody production, bacterial division and lysis

options.label: B
options.text: Binding/entry, reverse transcription, integration, replication/assembly and budding

options.label: D
options.text: Direct conversion of host protein into viral RNA without enzymes

options.label: E
options.text: DNA replication outside the host cell

questions.correctAnswerText: Binding/entry, reverse transcription, integration, replication/assembly and budding
questions.initialExplanation: HIV attaches to CD4 and co-receptors, fuses with the cell, converts viral RNA to DNA using reverse transcriptase, integrates viral DNA into the host genome, then produces and assembles new virions that bud from the cell.
questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Incorrect. Antibody production and bacterial division are unrelated. 
- B: Correct. This is the life cycle sequence in the standard clinical guidance. 
- C: Incorrect. This is not HIV replication. 
- D: Incorrect. Reverse transcriptase and integrase are essential viral enzymes.

- E: Incorrect. HIV uses intracellular reverse transcription and integration.
questions.highYieldPoints: NRTIs/NNRTIs inhibit reverse transcriptase; integrase inhibitors block integration; protease inhibitors interfere with viral maturation.

questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Incorrect. A single mild viral illness is common and nonspecific. 
- B: Incorrect. A small traumatic bruise alone is nonspecific.

- D: Incorrect. This is reassuring, though clinical screening depends on exposure risk.

- B: Incorrect. This is not the mechanism.

- C: Incorrect. Infants can produce antibodies; the problem is distinguishing infant-derived antibody from transferred maternal IgG. 
- D: Incorrect. HIV expresses viral proteins. 
- E: Correct. Maternal antibody persistence is the reason for false-positive infant serology.

questions.detailedExplanation:
- A: Incorrect. G6PD-related oxidative haemolysis is associated with Heinz bodies and bite cells rather than a positive DAT. 
- B: Incorrect. Iron deficiency causes microcytic hypochromic anaemia, not acute immune haemolysis. 
- C: Incorrect. Thalassaemia trait causes a chronic microcytic pattern and does not explain a positive DAT. 
- D: Correct. Antibody-coated red cells are removed by the reticuloendothelial system and may become spherocytes. 
- E: Incorrect. Aplastic anaemia is bone-marrow failure with reduced cell production, not peripheral immune destruction.
questions.highYieldPoints: A positive DAT supports immune haemolysis; interpret alongside reticulocytes, bilirubin, LDH and haptoglobin.

source.raw: Haematology — Immune Haemolytic Anaemia.
